title: The Choir of the Bell House
premise: Folklorist Kestrel Sandoval returns to the village of Hollowmere to record its dying songs, only to hear the church bell ring at midnight — a bell melted down in 1911, whose sound only he and the village's oldest residents can hear. The bell is a ledger: it tolls the names of things taken from the dead and never returned, and in 1974 the villagers stole a child's body from the Bell House to bury under their own church, cheating the house of its due. As the tolling grows closer together, Kestrel discovers his own family was among the thieves, and that the Bell House has chosen him — the last Sandoval — to carry the child home. In the end Kestrel exhumes the small coffin with the help of the outcasts who have become his found family, lays it in the Bell House as the village burns its own church rather than face judgment, and takes up residence as the house's keeper, finally part of a family that was never human but never let him go.
about_author: Oscar Okafor is a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing parish records across coastal England before turning to fiction. He writes horror about bureaucratic sins and the places that keep receipts.

chapters.title: Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Kestrel arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and ten years of rationalizations. An old woman, Maren, sings half a lullaby and stops cold when he asks her to repeat it. That night, from his rented room, he hears a single bell toll. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: unease dressed up as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Kestrel confirms in the parish archive that the bell was melted in 1911, yet every villager over seventy admits hearing it too — and all refuse to discuss 1974. He finds his own surname in the vestry minutes. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: the floor tilts; his family belongs to this.

chapters.title: The House That Keeps Accounts
chapters.summary: Kestrel explores the derelict Bell House on the hill and finds walls scratched with tally marks and a child's shoe on the mantel. The door closes behind him without being touched. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into being watched.

chapters.title: What Was Taken in '74
chapters.summary: Maren, drunk and terrified, tells him: in 1974 the village dug up a child buried in the Bell House garden and reburied her beneath the church altar so the house would stop calling their names. It worked for fifty years. POV: alternating Kestrel and Maren. Emotional beat: guilt inherited like property.

chapters.title: The Outcasts' Table
chapters.summary: The village's rejects — gravedigger Ivo, teenage runaway Petra, defrocked curate Halloran — take Kestrel in, having each heard the bell call their own names once. Over cards and cheap whisky they become his first real family. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: warmth as shelter before the storm.

chapters.title: Tolling Closer Together
chapters.summary: The bell begins ringing nightly, intervals shrinking. Villagers age visibly overnight; one dies with his mouth full of grave dirt. The churchwarden accuses Kestrel of bringing it back and organizes the village against him. POV: Kestrel and Petra. Emotional beat: siege mentality, allies cornered.

chapters.title: The Ledger Opens
chapters.summary: Inside the Bell House, Kestrel finds a ledger written in condensation on glass: names, dates, debts. His grandfather's signature is beside the entry for 'the child, Edith.' The house shows him 1974 — his grandfather holding the lantern while others dug. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: betrayal by the dead, grief for a man he mythologized.

chapters.title: Digging at the Altar
chapters.summary: Kestrel, Ivo, Petra, and Halloran break into the church at night to exhume Edith. The congregation, warned by the churchwarden, surrounds them mid-dig. Halloran stays above to hold the crowd with scripture turned against them while dirt flies below. POV: rotating among the four. Emotional beat: defiance — justice outside any law that protected the thieves.

chapters.title: The Procession Up the Hill
chapters.summary: Carrying the small coffin through a mob and a rising wind, Kestrel offers himself in place of punishment; the bell tolls once for each carrier, marking them. At the Bell House door it opens onto light the color of 1911. They lay Edith down; the tallies on the walls finish themselves. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into tenderness.

chapters.title: Keeper of the Bell
chapters.summary: The village burns its church rather than live under judgment, and half of them leave; those who remain come up the hill to leave flowers. Kestrel moves into the Bell House with Petra, Ivo, and Halloran — a household kept honest by a bell that rings only gratitude now. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: belonging, hard-won and strange.
